title: The Movement
bigQuestion: How did ordinary people, with no army and few votes, force a nation to change its laws, and what did it cost them?

story.title: The Open Casket
story.kicker: In September 1955 a Chicago mother made one decision about her son's funeral, and the whole country was forced to look.
paragraphs: Mamie Till-Mobley lived on the South Side of Chicago and worked as a clerk for the Air Force. In August 1955 she put her only child, fourteen-year-old Emmett Till, on the train south to visit relatives near Money, Mississippi. Emmett was a city kid who liked jokes and sharp clothes. His mother warned him that the rules were different in the Delta, that a Black boy had to be careful around white people. He promised he would be.

A few days later Emmett went into a small country store and, by the accounts that survive, said something or whistled at the white woman behind the counter. In the early hours of August 28, her husband Roy Bryant and his half-brother J. W. Milam took Emmett from his great-uncle's house at gunpoint. Three days later his body was pulled from the Tallahatchie River, beaten beyond recognition, a heavy cotton-gin fan tied to his neck with barbed wire. Mississippi officials wanted him buried fast, in the ground, out of sight.

Mamie Till-Mobley refused. She demanded the body be shipped home to Chicago. When the sealed box arrived at the rail station, she insisted it be opened. Then she made the decision the world remembers. There would be no closed lid and no makeup. She said she wanted the world to see what they had done to her boy. For four days in September, tens of thousands of Chicagoans filed past the glass-covered casket at Roberts Temple Church of God in Christ on State Street. Jet, a Black magazine published in Chicago, printed the photograph. It traveled everywhere.

Later that month an all-white jury in Sumner, Mississippi, took about an hour to find Bryant and Milam not guilty. The next year, safe from a second trial, the two men sold their confession to a magazine for money. No one was ever punished. But something had shifted. In Montgomery, Alabama, a seamstress named Rosa Parks later said she was thinking of Emmett Till when she refused to give up her bus seat that December. A generation of Black teenagers who saw the photo in Jet would fill the sit-ins and the Freedom Rides five years later.

This chapter is about that generation and the movement they built. It began in courtrooms and church basements, moved into buses, lunch counters and jail cells, and ended in the laws of the United States. It also came north, to Chicago, where it met a different kind of wall. Through all of it runs the question Mamie Till-Mobley answered in 1955: what happens when people refuse to let injustice stay hidden?
story.think: Mamie Till-Mobley could have buried her son quietly. Why do you think making the public look was a form of power, and what did it cost her to use it?

lessons.title: Brown v. Board of Education
lessons.mainIdea: In 1954 the Supreme Court ruled that racially segregated public schools are unconstitutional, overturning the separate-but-equal rule from 1896.
reading: Every school morning in Topeka, Kansas, a girl named Linda Brown walked past a white elementary school a few blocks from her house to catch a bus to a Black school across town. In 1950 her father, Oliver Brown, tried to enroll her in the closer school and was turned away. The Brown family joined a lawsuit organized by the NAACP, the nation's oldest civil rights organization. Similar cases from South Carolina, Virginia, Delaware and Washington, D.C., were bundled with it. Together they became Brown v. Board of Education.

The law they were fighting went back to 1896. In Plessy v. Ferguson the Supreme Court had ruled that a state could require separate railroad cars for Black and white passengers as long as the cars were roughly equal. That decision became the legal backbone of *segregation*, the system of separating people by race in schools, parks, buses, restrooms and hospitals across the South. In practice the facilities were rarely equal. Black schools often had used textbooks, no buses and half the money per student.

The NAACP's lead lawyer, Thurgood Marshall, argued that even if the buildings were identical, forced separation itself did harm. His team offered evidence from social scientists, including a study in which many Black children chose a white doll over a Black one when asked which was nicer. On May 17, 1954, Chief Justice Earl Warren read a *unanimous* decision, all nine justices agreeing. Separate educational facilities, he wrote, are inherently unequal. Segregated schools violated the Fourteenth Amendment's promise of equal protection.

A decision is not the same as a change. The next year the Court ordered schools to desegregate with all deliberate speed, a vague phrase that many Southern districts read as permission to wait. Some states closed schools rather than mix them. In 1957 the governor of Arkansas used the National Guard to block nine Black students from Little Rock Central High School, and President Eisenhower sent Army paratroopers to walk them in. Ten years after Brown, most Black children in the Deep South still attended all-Black schools. The ruling gave the movement a legal foundation. People would have to build on it.

words.d: the forced separation of people by race in schools, transportation and public places
agreed to by everyone; in Brown, all nine justices voted the same way
the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, whose lawyers led the school cases
the Fourteenth Amendment's rule that states must apply the law equally to all people

look.title: The Court Speaks
look.text: We conclude that in the field of public education the doctrine of 'separate but equal' has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.
look.cite: Chief Justice Earl Warren, Brown v. Board of Education, U.S. Supreme Court, May 17, 1954
look.prompt: The Court did not say the Black schools were worse. It said separation itself was unequal. Why does that argument matter more than comparing buildings?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Brown v. Board of Education?
choices: Segregated public schools are unconstitutional
Black schools must receive equal funding
Each state may choose whether to segregate
Segregation on buses is illegal
check.why: The Court ruled that separate schools are inherently unequal and violate the Fourteenth Amendment.

check.q: Which earlier case had allowed separate-but-equal facilities?
choices: Marbury v. Madison
Plessy v. Ferguson
Dred Scott v. Sandford
Little Rock v. Arkansas
check.why: Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 approved separate railroad cars and became the basis for segregation laws.

check.q: Why did many Southern schools stay segregated for years after 1954?
choices: The ruling applied only to Kansas
Black families chose not to enroll
The Court allowed desegregation at 'all deliberate speed' and many districts stalled
Congress overturned the decision
check.why: The vague timeline let districts delay, and some states resisted openly until federal force or later laws pushed them.

lessons.title: Emmett Till and Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: The murder of a Chicago teenager in Mississippi in 1955, and his mother's decision to show it, turned a private crime into a national reckoning.
reading: By 1955 Chicago's South Side was home to hundreds of thousands of Black families who had come north in the Great Migration. Many still had relatives in Mississippi and Arkansas and sent their children south each summer. That is why Emmett Till, fourteen years old and raised on Chicago's streets, was in the Mississippi Delta in August 1955. The rules there were enforced not only by law but by the constant threat of violence. A Black person who crossed a line could be beaten or killed, and the killers almost never faced a court.

That threat was called *lynching*: murder by a mob or a group, outside the law, meant to terrorize a whole community. Between the 1880s and the 1950s thousands of Black Americans were lynched across the South, often in public, sometimes with photographs sold as postcards. Congress debated anti-lynching bills for decades and Southern senators blocked every one. Emmett Till's murder fit an old pattern. What broke the pattern was what his mother did next.

Mamie Till-Mobley's open casket in Chicago and the photographs in Jet magazine reached Black homes across the country. Many people later said that image was the moment they decided to act. The trial in Mississippi added fuel. Emmett's great-uncle, Mose Wright, a sharecropper in his sixties, stood up in a Southern courtroom, pointed at the two white defendants and identified them as the men who took the boy. It was an act of enormous courage. The jury freed the defendants anyway.

The case did not change Mississippi law. It changed what people were willing to accept. Mamie Till-Mobley spent the rest of her life speaking about her son and became a Chicago public school teacher. In 2022 Congress finally made lynching a federal crime, and named the law after Emmett Till. Roberts Temple church still stands on State Street, and the Till home on South St. Lawrence Avenue is now a Chicago landmark. How we know this story is itself part of it: the photographs, the trial transcript, the magazine, and the words of the witnesses who dared to speak.

words.d: murder by a group outside the law, used for decades to terrorize Black communities
the movement of millions of Black Southerners to Northern cities like Chicago between about 1910 and 1970
a farmer who worked someone else's land in exchange for a share of the crop, often trapped in debt

look.title: The Witness Stand
look.text: Picture the courtroom in Sumner, Mississippi, in September 1955. Ceiling fans turn in the heat. Every face in the jury box is white. A sixty-four-year-old Black farmer in a clean pressed suit is asked whether he can identify the men who came to his house. He stands, raises his arm and points. He knows he cannot safely go home after this. That night his family leaves Mississippi for Chicago.
look.prompt: Mose Wright's testimony did not win the case. Why might historians still call it one of the most important moments of the trial?

check.q: Why was Emmett Till, a Chicago boy, in Mississippi in 1955?
choices: His family had moved back south
He was attending school there
He was working on a cotton farm
He was visiting relatives, as many children of the Great Migration did
check.why: Many Chicago families kept ties to the South and sent children to visit relatives in summer.

check.q: What was the main purpose of lynching as described in the lesson?
choices: To terrorize an entire community into obeying the racial order
To punish people convicted in court
To settle disputes between white families
To enforce federal law
check.why: Lynching was murder outside the law meant to frighten all Black people, not just the victim.

check.q: What did Mamie Till-Mobley's open casket accomplish?
choices: It convinced the jury to convict
It forced the nation to see the violence and moved many people to act
It ended segregation in Mississippi
It led Congress to pass an anti-lynching law that year
check.why: The photographs did not change the verdict, but they reached millions and became a spark for the movement.

lessons.title: Montgomery Walks
lessons.mainIdea: The 1955 Montgomery bus boycott showed that a whole Black community, organized and patient, could defeat segregation with its feet and its dollars.
reading: On Thursday, December 1, 1955, Rosa Parks finished her shift as a seamstress at a Montgomery, Alabama, department store and boarded a bus home. City law reserved the front rows for white riders, and the driver could order Black riders to give up seats further back when the white section filled. When the driver told Parks to move, she said no. She was arrested. Parks was not simply tired, as the story is often told. She was a longtime secretary of the local NAACP and had trained in organizing that summer.

That night Jo Ann Robinson, a college English professor who led the Women's Political Council, stayed up copying a flyer on a mimeograph machine. It called on Black riders to stay off the buses on Monday, the day of Parks's trial. Ministers announced it from every pulpit on Sunday. On Monday the buses ran almost empty. That evening thousands packed a church meeting and chose a twenty-six-year-old new pastor, Martin Luther King Jr., to lead a new organization, the Montgomery Improvement Association. They voted to keep the *boycott* going.

The boycott lasted 381 days. Black residents were about three quarters of the bus company's riders, so their absence emptied its cash box. People walked miles in every weather. Churches ran a carpool of about three hundred cars. Black taxi drivers charged bus fare. White employers who supported segregation found themselves driving their maids to work. The city fought back: it fined the carpool drivers, indicted King and dozens of others under an old anti-boycott law, and someone bombed King's house with his wife and baby inside.

Victory came from two directions at once. The economic pressure hurt, but the legal blow came from a separate lawsuit, Browder v. Gayle, filed by four Black women riders. In November 1956 the Supreme Court affirmed that bus segregation in Montgomery was unconstitutional. On December 21, 1956, Black riders returned and sat where they chose. The lessons were clear to organizers everywhere: mass participation, careful planning, economic pressure, a court case running alongside, and a strict commitment to *nonviolence* even under attack.

words.d: refusing to buy from or use a business until it changes, as a form of protest
a strategy of protest that refuses to strike back, even when attacked, in order to expose injustice
a hand-cranked copying machine used before photocopiers to print flyers
the group formed in December 1955 to run the bus boycott, led by Martin Luther King Jr.

look.title: Who Rides the Bus
look.text: In 1955 Montgomery had about fifty thousand Black residents. Most did not own cars and rode the city buses to work, to school and to shop. The bus company depended on their fares for roughly three quarters of its income. Now imagine three quarters of a store's customers vanishing on the same Monday morning and not coming back for a year.
look.prompt: Why did economic pressure work in Montgomery when moral arguments alone had failed for decades? What did the boycott require from each rider, day after day?

check.q: Which statement about Rosa Parks is supported by the lesson?
choices: She was a random rider who was simply tired
She was a trained NAACP activist who chose not to move
She was the first person arrested for bus segregation
She led the boycott organization
check.why: Parks was the local NAACP secretary and had trained in organizing that summer. King led the MIA.

check.q: What finally ended bus segregation in Montgomery?
choices: The bus company changed its policy after losing money
The city council repealed the law
A Supreme Court ruling in the Browder v. Gayle lawsuit
The state of Alabama ordered integration
check.why: The boycott applied pressure, but the legal end came when the Supreme Court affirmed that the bus law was unconstitutional.

check.q: Why did the boycott depend on carpools and taxis?
choices: To protest gasoline prices
To carry protesters to other cities
To keep bus fares low
So people without cars could still get to work for over a year
check.why: Most Black riders had no car. The carpool of about three hundred vehicles made the year-long boycott possible.

lessons.title: Sitting In
lessons.mainIdea: Beginning in 1960, Black college students used sit-ins at segregated lunch counters to take the movement into their own hands.
reading: On February 1, 1960, four freshmen from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical College walked into the Woolworth's store in Greensboro, bought some school supplies, and then sat down at the lunch counter, which served only white customers. They asked for coffee. They were refused, and they stayed until closing. The next day they came back with more students. Within a week hundreds were sitting in. Within two months *sit-ins* had spread to more than fifty cities across the South.

The tactic was simple and hard. Sit quietly, dress well, bring a book, ask to be served. Do not hit back when someone pours ketchup on your head or burns you with a cigarette. Be arrested politely and fill the jails. In Nashville, a minister named James Lawson had spent months training students, including Diane Nash and John Lewis, in the discipline of nonviolent *direct action*: confronting an unjust rule in person instead of waiting for a court. They practiced being shoved and insulted until they could take it without flinching.

The sit-ins mattered because of who led them. The students were not waiting for the NAACP's lawyers or the ministers of Montgomery. In April 1960 Ella Baker, a veteran organizer who distrusted leader-centered movements, helped them form their own group, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, known as SNCC. It would send young organizers into the most dangerous counties of Mississippi and Alabama for the rest of the decade.

The results came fast by the movement's standards. Woolworth's in Greensboro served its first Black customers at the counter in July 1960. Nashville's downtown stores desegregated that spring after the mayor, confronted on the courthouse steps by Diane Nash, admitted in public that segregation was wrong. Sit-ins did not end all segregation, but they proved a lesson: a business that depends on customers cannot afford a daily scene at its counter, and young people could create that scene anywhere.

words.d: a protest in which people sit in a place they are barred from and refuse to leave
confronting an unjust rule in person, such as a boycott or sit-in, instead of waiting for courts or officials
the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, founded by students in 1960

look.title: Training Night in Nashville
look.text: A church basement, fall 1959. Students take turns sitting on folding chairs set up like a lunch counter. Others play the role of hecklers: they shout, shove, pull a chair out from under a friend. The rule is that the students on the chairs may not respond. Afterward they talk about what made them angriest and how they held still.
look.prompt: Why did the Nashville students practice being attacked before they ever sat down at a real counter? What might have happened without the training?

check.q: What happened at the Greensboro Woolworth's on February 1, 1960?
choices: Four Black college students sat at a whites-only lunch counter and refused to leave
Store workers went on strike
Police closed the store
The store voluntarily integrated its counter
check.why: The four freshmen asked for coffee, were refused, and stayed. Their action spread across the South.

check.q: What was new about the sit-in movement compared with Brown v. Board?
choices: It relied on federal judges
Students themselves confronted segregation directly instead of waiting for courts
It took place only in the North
It used armed self-defense
check.why: Direct action put students face to face with the rule they opposed, at the counter itself.

check.q: Which organization did the students found in April 1960?
choices: The NAACP
The Montgomery Improvement Association
SNCC, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee
The Congress of Racial Equality
check.why: With Ella Baker's help, sit-in students formed SNCC to run their own campaigns.

lessons.title: The Freedom Rides
lessons.mainIdea: In 1961 integrated groups rode buses into the Deep South to test a federal ruling, and the violence they met forced the government to enforce it.
reading: The Supreme Court had already ruled that segregation in bus stations serving interstate travel was illegal. The problem was that no one in the South enforced it. In May 1961 the Congress of Racial Equality, or CORE, led by James Farmer, decided to test the ruling. Thirteen riders, Black and white together, boarded two buses in Washington, D.C., bound for New Orleans. They planned to use the whites-only waiting rooms and restrooms at each stop. They expected trouble and got it.

On May 14, Mother's Day, one bus was attacked outside Anniston, Alabama. A mob slashed the tires and, when the bus stopped, threw a firebomb through a window. The riders escaped with smoke in their lungs just before the bus exploded into flames. The other bus reached Birmingham, where a mob armed with pipes and chains beat the riders while police stayed away. A photograph of the burning bus went around the world. CORE, its riders in the hospital, decided to stop.

The Nashville students refused to let the ride end. Diane Nash argued that if violence could stop a Freedom Ride, the movement was finished. New riders, John Lewis among them, went to Birmingham and then to Montgomery, where another mob beat them on the station platform. Attorney General Robert Kennedy, the president's brother, sent federal marshals. When the riders reached Jackson, Mississippi, they were arrested and sent to the state penitentiary. More kept coming all summer. More than three hundred people served time in Mississippi prisons for the crime of sitting in the wrong waiting room.

The Freedom Rides won on a technical point that changed daily life. In September 1961, under pressure from the Kennedy administration, the Interstate Commerce Commission ordered the signs down in every interstate bus and train station. The rides also taught the movement something about power. Segregationist violence, when captured on camera, embarrassed the United States in front of the world during the Cold War. That embarrassment could move a president who would rather not be moved.

words.d: the Congress of Racial Equality, a civil rights group founded in Chicago in 1942 that organized the Freedom Rides
crossing state lines; the federal government regulates interstate travel
the Black and white activists who rode buses into the South in 1961 to challenge segregated stations
officers of the U.S. Justice Department who can be sent to enforce federal law

look.title: The Photograph From Anniston
look.text: A Greyhound bus sits on the shoulder of a two-lane Alabama highway, black smoke pouring from its windows. Young people in their Sunday clothes sit on the grass coughing. Picture that image printed the next morning in newspapers in London, Delhi, Lagos and Moscow, at a moment when the United States claimed to lead the free world.
look.prompt: Why might a single photograph have pushed the Kennedy administration harder than a year of polite requests? Who was the real audience for the Freedom Rides?

check.q: What were the Freedom Riders testing in 1961?
choices: Whether Southern schools would admit Black students
Whether buses would let Black riders sit in front
Whether restaurants would serve them
Whether a Supreme Court ruling against segregated interstate bus stations would be enforced
check.why: The ruling already existed; the riders wanted to see if the government would make the South obey it.

check.q: Why did the Nashville students insist on continuing after Anniston and Birmingham?
choices: They believed letting violence stop the ride would show that violence works
CORE ordered them to
They wanted to reach New Orleans for a festival
They thought the mobs had given up
check.why: Diane Nash argued the movement would be dead if a mob could end a protest.

check.q: What concrete result did the Freedom Rides produce?
choices: Mississippi repealed its segregation laws
The Interstate Commerce Commission ordered segregation signs removed from interstate stations
Congress passed the Civil Rights Act
Bus companies stopped running routes in the South
check.why: In September 1961 the ICC ordered all interstate bus and train stations to desegregate.

lessons.title: Birmingham, 1963
lessons.mainIdea: In Birmingham, the movement chose the most segregated city in America and let the nation watch police attack children, which pushed a president to act.
reading: By early 1963 King's organization, the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, needed a win. A long campaign in Albany, Georgia, had fizzled because the police chief there arrested protesters calmly and out of sight. Birmingham, Alabama, was chosen because it was the opposite. Its public safety commissioner, Eugene Connor, known as Bull, was a hot-tempered segregationist. The city had seen so many bombings of Black homes and churches that people called it Bombingham. Organizers believed that if Connor reacted the way he always did, the cameras would show the country what segregation really was.

The campaign began in April with marches and sit-ins downtown, and arrests followed. King himself was jailed on Good Friday. In his cell he wrote a long letter on scraps of newspaper and toilet paper, answering white clergymen who had called the protests unwise and untimely. He argued that people who have waited more than three hundred years are told to wait too easily by those who have never had to. The Letter from Birmingham Jail became the movement's most famous defense of nonviolent direct action and of breaking unjust laws openly and lovingly, ready to accept the penalty.

By May, adult volunteers were running out. Organizer James Bevel proposed sending students. On May 2 more than a thousand children, some as young as six, marched out of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church and were arrested. The next day Connor turned high-pressure fire hoses on them, strong enough to strip bark from trees, and released police dogs. The photographs and television footage shocked the country. Within days Birmingham's business leaders agreed to desegregate downtown stores and hire Black workers.

President Kennedy had avoided a civil rights bill for two years. On June 11, 1963, he went on national television and called civil rights a moral issue as old as the Scriptures and as clear as the Constitution. He asked Congress for a law ending segregation in public places. Hours later, in Jackson, Mississippi, NAACP leader Medgar Evers was shot dead in his driveway. In September a bomb at the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church killed four girls at Sunday school. Birmingham had forced the question. It had not answered the violence.

words.d: the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, a group of ministers led by Martin Luther King Jr.
in King's argument, a law that a majority forces on a minority without following it themselves
the May 1963 marches in Birmingham in which more than a thousand students were arrested

look.title: A Moral Issue
look.text: We are confronted primarily with a moral issue. It is as old as the Scriptures and is as clear as the American Constitution.
look.cite: President John F. Kennedy, televised address on civil rights, June 11, 1963
look.prompt: Kennedy had treated civil rights as a political problem to manage. What had changed by June 1963 that made him call it a moral issue instead?

check.q: Why did the SCLC choose Birmingham for its 1963 campaign?
choices: It was the least segregated city in the South
Its leaders had promised to negotiate
Organizers expected Bull Connor to respond violently in front of cameras
It had a large Black voting population
check.why: After Albany failed quietly, organizers wanted a place where segregation's violence would be visible.

check.q: What was the central argument of the Letter from Birmingham Jail?
choices: Protesters should wait for the courts
Violence is sometimes justified
White clergy should leave the South
People told to wait for centuries have the right to break unjust laws openly and accept the penalty
check.why: King defended nonviolent direct action and open civil disobedience against those who called the protests untimely.

check.q: What was the most immediate national effect of the images from Birmingham?
choices: President Kennedy publicly asked Congress for a civil rights law
Bull Connor was arrested
The Supreme Court ended segregation
Alabama integrated its schools
check.why: Within weeks, Kennedy gave his June 11 address and sent a bill to Congress.

lessons.title: The March on Washington
lessons.mainIdea: On August 28, 1963, about a quarter of a million people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial to demand jobs and freedom, and made the movement a national majority cause.
reading: The idea was old. In 1941 A. Philip Randolph, leader of the Black railroad porters' union, had threatened a march on Washington to demand defense jobs, and President Roosevelt had opened war plants to Black workers to head it off. In 1963 Randolph, now in his seventies, revived the plan, and the organizing fell to Bayard Rustin, a brilliant pacifist strategist who had been kept in the background because he was gay and a former Communist. Rustin had eight weeks to move a small city's worth of people into the capital and out again in one day.

The full name was the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom. The demands were economic as well as legal: a two-dollar minimum wage, a federal jobs program, an end to discrimination in hiring, and passage of Kennedy's civil rights bill. On August 28 roughly 250,000 people arrived by train, bus and car, about a quarter of them white. Labor unions, churches and civil rights groups marched together. Kennedy, who had worried about violence, watched on television as the crowd stayed orderly and left the Mall spotless.

The speeches ran all afternoon. John Lewis, the twenty-three-year-old chairman of SNCC, had to soften a draft that called Kennedy's bill too little, too late. Gospel singer Mahalia Jackson, who lived in Chicago, sang. Then King, the last speaker, set aside his prepared text partway through and spoke of a dream in which children would be judged by their character and not their color. The speech, delivered in the shadow of the Lincoln statue on the hundredth anniversary of the Emancipation Proclamation, became the best known words of the century.

Historians point out what the memory leaves out. The day was organized by a union leader and a gay pacifist, not only ministers. No woman gave a major speech, though women like Daisy Bates and Rosa Parks were on the platform. The jobs demands were mostly not met. And within three weeks the Birmingham church bombing showed that words at the Lincoln Memorial had not reached Alabama. Still, the march did what marches are for. It showed the country and Congress that the movement was large, disciplined and impossible to ignore.

words.d: a person who opposes all war and violence on principle
Lincoln's 1863 order declaring enslaved people in rebel states free
the lowest hourly pay a law allows an employer to offer

look.title: Who Came to the Mall
rows: Marchers at the Lincoln Memorial, Aug. 28, 1963
Chartered buses that arrived that morning
look.cite: National Park Service and contemporary press accounts, rounded
look.prompt: Kennedy feared a riot. What do the numbers of buses and arrests together tell you about how the march was organized, and why did that matter to Congress?

check.q: What did the full name of the march show about its goals?
choices: It was only about voting rights
It demanded jobs and economic fairness as well as an end to segregation
It was a religious event
It sought to end the Cold War
check.why: The March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom included demands for a higher minimum wage and fair hiring.

check.q: Who was the chief organizer who planned the logistics in eight weeks?
choices: Martin Luther King Jr.
John Lewis
Bayard Rustin
Mahalia Jackson
check.why: Rustin, a pacifist strategist, ran the planning, while Randolph was the elder statesman who called the march.

check.q: Which criticism of the march do historians raise in the lesson?
choices: Too few people attended
It turned violent
It ignored the civil rights bill
No woman gave a major speech and the jobs demands were mostly not met
check.why: The lesson notes women were on the platform but not at the microphone, and the economic goals fell short.

lessons.title: Freedom Summer
lessons.mainIdea: In 1964 civil rights workers brought hundreds of volunteers into Mississippi to register voters and open schools, at the cost of three lives and dozens of bombings.
reading: In 1964 Mississippi had the lowest share of Black registered voters in the country, about seven percent of those eligible. The tools of exclusion were the *literacy test*, in which a county clerk could ask a Black applicant to explain any section of the state constitution and fail them for any reason, the *poll tax*, and plain fear. A sharecropper who tried to register might be fired, evicted or shot at. SNCC organizer Bob Moses had spent three years in the state and had watched local people beaten and killed for trying.

Moses and the coalition of groups called COFO made a hard calculation. If Black Mississippians died, the country did not notice. If white college students from the North were hurt, it would. So Freedom Summer recruited about a thousand volunteers, most of them white students, to spend the summer registering voters and teaching in Freedom Schools. On June 21, the first day, three workers vanished near Philadelphia, Mississippi: James Chaney, a Black Mississippian, and Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner, two white New Yorkers. Their bodies were found in an earthen dam in August. Local police and Klansmen had murdered them.

The summer went on. Volunteers lived with Black families who risked everything to host them. More than thirty Black churches were bombed or burned. Freedom Schools taught Black history and the Constitution to thousands of children who had never seen either in a Mississippi classroom. Registration gains were small because the clerks did not budge, but the project built something else: the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, an open party to challenge the all-white official Democrats.

In August the MFDP sent a delegation to the Democratic National Convention in Atlantic City and asked to be seated in place of the segregationists. Fannie Lou Hamer, a former sharecropper who had been beaten in jail for trying to register, testified on live television about what had been done to her. President Johnson, afraid of losing the South, cut in with a press conference to knock her off the air, but the networks replayed her that night. The party offered the MFDP two seats without votes. They refused. Many young activists left Atlantic City convinced that appeals to the conscience of the powerful were not enough.

words.d: a reading or civics exam used by Southern clerks to keep Black citizens from registering to vote
a fee that had to be paid before voting, banned in federal elections by the Twenty-fourth Amendment in 1964
summer schools run in 1964 that taught Mississippi Black children history, civics and reading
the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, formed in 1964 to challenge the all-white state party

look.title: Fannie Lou Hamer in Atlantic City
look.text: Hamer told the convention committee that she had been fired from the plantation where she had worked for eighteen years on the same day she tried to register, that she had been jailed and beaten with a blackjack in Winona, and that she wanted to know whether this was America, the land of the free and the home of the brave.
look.cite: Fannie Lou Hamer, testimony to the Democratic National Convention credentials committee, August 22, 1964 (paraphrased)
look.prompt: Hamer was a sharecropper with a sixth-grade education speaking to lawyers and senators. Why was her testimony more powerful than a report with the same facts?

check.q: Why did Freedom Summer organizers recruit mostly white Northern volunteers?
choices: They calculated that violence against white students would draw national attention that violence against Black Mississippians had not
Black students were not interested
White students knew Mississippi better
Federal law required it
check.why: Bob Moses and COFO made the painful judgment that the country would notice white victims.

check.q: What happened to James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner?
choices: They were arrested and served a year in prison
They were murdered by police and Klansmen on the first day of the project
They led the MFDP delegation

Federal troops for Mississippi
To be seated in place of the all-white Mississippi delegation

check.why: The MFDP argued that the official delegation was chosen by excluding Black voters and should be replaced.

lessons.title: Selma and the Bridge
lessons.mainIdea: The 1965 Selma campaign, and the attack on marchers at the Edmund Pettus Bridge, produced the Voting Rights Act within five months.
reading: Selma, Alabama, sat in Dallas County, where Black residents were about half the population and about two percent of the registered voters. The county registrar opened two days a month and failed almost every Black applicant. In January 1965 King and the SCLC joined SNCC organizers already in town for a campaign aimed squarely at the vote. Marchers lined up at the courthouse and were arrested by the hundreds. In February, in nearby Marion, a state trooper shot a young man named Jimmie Lee Jackson as he tried to shield his mother. He died days later.

Activists planned a march from Selma to the state capital in Montgomery, fifty-four miles, to protest the killing. On Sunday, March 7, about six hundred marchers led by John Lewis and Hosea Williams walked out of Selma and over the Edmund Pettus Bridge, named for a Confederate general and Klan leader. On the far side waited state troopers and county deputies on horseback. They gave the marchers two minutes, then attacked with clubs and tear gas. Lewis's skull was fractured. Television networks interrupted their Sunday evening programs to show the footage. The day became known as Bloody Sunday.

Hundreds of clergy and ordinary citizens flew to Selma in response. A white minister from Boston, James Reeb, was beaten to death on a Selma street. On March 15 President Lyndon Johnson addressed a joint session of Congress, called the events at Selma a turning point like Lexington and Concord, and told the lawmakers that the cause of Black Americans must be everyone's cause. Then he closed with the movement's own words, and we shall overcome. Watching on television, King wept. On March 21, under federal protection, the march finally set out. Five days later about twenty-five thousand people reached the capitol in Montgomery.

The night the march ended, Klansmen shot and killed Viola Liuzzo, a Detroit mother of five who had driven marchers home. The bill moved anyway. On August 6, 1965, Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act. Selma showed the pattern of the whole movement in one town: local people who had been organizing for years, national leaders who brought attention, violence that the nation could not look away from, and a law that followed. It also showed the cost, paid mostly by people whose names are on no monument.

words.d: the county official who decided who could be added to the voting rolls
March 7, 1965, when Alabama troopers attacked voting rights marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge
a meeting of both houses of Congress together, usually to hear the president

look.title: Two Minutes on the Bridge
look.text: Imagine standing at the crest of the bridge on that Sunday afternoon. The Alabama River is below you. Ahead, a line of blue-helmeted troopers blocks all four lanes, and men on horseback wait behind them. You are told to turn around. You have already decided you will not. Next to you a woman grips her purse; behind you a boy of fifteen. The gas masks go on.
look.prompt: The marchers knew what was likely to happen and walked anyway. What were they counting on, and what does it mean that they turned out to be right?

choices: It had a friendly sheriff
It was the state capital
Its Black population was large and its registered Black voters were almost none
It had already passed a voting law
check.why: Dallas County's Black residents were about half the population but about two percent of registered voters.

choices: The marchers reached Montgomery
President Johnson signed the Voting Rights Act
Jimmie Lee Jackson was shot
State troopers attacked marchers on the Edmund Pettus Bridge with clubs and tear gas
check.why: Bloody Sunday was broadcast that evening and brought hundreds of supporters to Selma.

choices: He addressed Congress, adopted the movement's words, and pushed the Voting Rights Act through by August
He sent troops to stop the march
He waited for the courts
He ordered a new election in Alabama
check.why: Johnson's March 15 speech to Congress ended with 'we shall overcome,' and he signed the act on August 6, 1965.

lessons.title: Two Laws That Changed the Country
lessons.mainIdea: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 put the federal government behind equal treatment and the ballot, and the numbers changed fast.
reading: After Kennedy's assassination in November 1963, Lyndon Johnson, a Texan who had spent decades in Congress, took up the civil rights bill as his own. Southern senators launched a *filibuster*, endless speeches meant to keep the bill from ever coming to a vote, that ran for more than two months. Johnson and Senate leaders of both parties gathered the two-thirds needed to shut off debate. The Civil Rights Act was signed on July 2, 1964. It banned segregation in restaurants, hotels, theaters and other public places, outlawed discrimination in hiring based on race, color, religion, sex or national origin, and let the government cut off funds to schools that stayed segregated.

The word sex was added to the employment section by a Virginia congressman who opposed the bill and may have hoped to sink it. It stayed. The new law's job provisions, enforced by a new Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, would become the main legal weapon of the women's movement over the next decade. A law written for one struggle turned out to be a tool for many.

The Voting Rights Act of 1965 attacked the machinery of exclusion directly. It banned literacy tests in states with a history of discrimination, sent federal examiners to register voters where local clerks refused, and required those states to get federal approval, called *preclearance*, before changing any voting rule. The effect was immediate. In Mississippi, Black registration rose from about seven percent of eligible adults in 1964 to nearly sixty percent by 1968. Across the South, Black sheriffs, mayors and legislators began to win office for the first time since the 1870s.

Both laws have had long afterlives. Courts have spent decades deciding what the Civil Rights Act's ban on discrimination covers. In 2013 the Supreme Court, in Shelby County v. Holder, struck down the formula that decided which states needed preclearance, saying it was based on outdated data. Several states changed voting rules soon after. Whether those changes protect elections or restrict voters is argued today along party lines. What the evidence of 1965 shows plainly is that when the federal government enforced the right to vote, millions of citizens used it.

words.d: using unlimited debate in the Senate to block a vote on a bill
the Voting Rights Act rule that certain states had to get federal approval before changing voting laws
the federal agency created in 1964 to enforce the ban on job discrimination
treating people worse because of their race, sex, religion or other group identity

look.title: Black Voter Registration Before and After the Act

look.prompt: The Voting Rights Act became law in August 1965. What in the numbers tells you that the barrier had been the rules and their enforcers rather than the voters?

check.q: What did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 do?
choices: It abolished literacy tests
It banned segregation in public places and discrimination in hiring
It gave women the vote

check.why: The 1964 act covered public accommodations and employment; voting rules came in the 1965 act.

Registration fell as voters lost interest

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Shelby County v. Holder in 2013?

lessons.title: King Comes to Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: In 1966 the movement turned north to Chicago, where segregation was enforced not by law but by housing practices, and found it far harder to break.
reading: In January 1966 Martin Luther King Jr. rented an apartment in North Lawndale on Chicago's West Side and moved in with his family. The building was run-down and cold; the landlord rushed to fix it once reporters arrived. King had come at the invitation of local organizers to launch the Chicago Freedom Movement. The target was not a law. Chicago had no segregation statute. Yet the city was among the most segregated in the country, and Black families paid more for worse housing than white families paid for better.

The tools were quieter than Bull Connor's dogs. For decades federal maps had marked Black neighborhoods in red as bad risks for loans, a practice called *redlining*, so banks would not lend there. Real estate agents steered Black buyers away from white areas. Because they could not get mortgages, Black families bought homes on contract, paying installments for years with no ownership until the last payment and losing everything if they missed one. White homeowners' groups and, at times, mobs made sure the boundaries held. Public schools followed the neighborhoods, so they were segregated too.

In July 1966 King addressed a rally at Soldier Field, then marched to City Hall and taped the movement's demands to the door. In August marchers walked into Marquette Park on the Southwest Side to demand open housing. Thousands of white residents met them with rocks, bottles and Nazi signs. King was struck in the head by a rock and said he had never seen mobs as hateful, even in Mississippi and Alabama. Late that summer Mayor Richard J. Daley signed an agreement promising fair housing steps. King left. Most of the promises went unkept.

The Chicago campaign is often called a failure, and by the measure of Birmingham it was. But it shifted the movement's understanding. Northern segregation was built into banking, real estate and city planning, and no single law could undo it. In April 1968, days after King was assassinated in Memphis, Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, which banned discrimination in selling and renting homes. Chicago's housing patterns, though, still trace the old redlining maps. You can see them in the census today.

words.d: marking Black neighborhoods on maps as too risky for loans, which cut them off from mortgages
the right to buy or rent a home anywhere without discrimination
buying a home in installments with no ownership until the last payment, which let sellers evict buyers who missed one
the 1968 federal law banning discrimination in the sale and rental of housing

look.cite: U.S. Census, rounded to the nearest thousand
look.prompt: The Black population nearly quadrupled in thirty years while the neighborhoods open to Black families barely grew. What would that do to rents, crowding and the pressure at the boundary lines?

choices: It was enforced through housing practices like redlining rather than by law

check.why: Chicago had no segregation law, but lending, real estate and city practices kept neighborhoods separated.

Banks charged very low interest

lessons.title: Malcolm X and Black Power
lessons.mainIdea: Malcolm X and the Black Power movement argued that self-defense, pride and control of Black communities mattered as much as integration.
reading: Malcolm Little was born in Omaha in 1925. His father, a preacher who followed Marcus Garvey, died violently when Malcolm was six; his mother was committed to a mental hospital; Malcolm drifted to Boston and Harlem and into prison for burglary at twenty. There he read constantly and joined the Nation of Islam, a Black religious movement led by Elijah Muhammad from its headquarters on Chicago's South Side. He took the name Malcolm X, the X standing for the African family name that slavery had erased.

Through the 1950s and early 1960s Malcolm X became the Nation's most powerful speaker. He rejected the goal of integration and the strategy of nonviolence. Why, he asked, should Black people beg to sit beside those who hated them, and why should they let themselves be beaten without striking back? He called for *self-defense*, Black-owned businesses and pride in African history. Many civil rights leaders considered him dangerous. Many young Black people in Northern cities, where the movement's Southern victories changed little, found him the only leader saying what they felt.

In 1964 Malcolm broke with the Nation of Islam and made the pilgrimage to Mecca, where he prayed beside Muslims of every color and began to revise his views on race. He founded a new organization and started talking with civil rights leaders he had once mocked. On February 21, 1965, he was shot dead while speaking at the Audubon Ballroom in New York. Three members of the Nation of Islam were convicted; two of them were cleared decades later. His autobiography, published that year, became one of the most read American books of the century.

In June 1966, during a march through Mississippi, SNCC's new chairman Stokely Carmichael gave the mood a name: *Black Power*. It meant different things to different people, from electing Black officials to building separate institutions. In Oakland that October, Huey Newton and Bobby Seale founded the Black Panther Party, which patrolled police with loaded guns, which was legal in California, and ran free breakfast programs for children. In Chicago the Panthers' twenty-one-year-old leader, Fred Hampton, built alliances with poor white and Latino groups. On December 4, 1969, Chicago police killed him in his bed during a pre-dawn raid coordinated with the FBI. Black Power frightened much of white America. It also reshaped how Black Americans saw themselves.

words.d: using force to protect yourself when attacked; Malcolm X argued Black Americans had that right
a slogan from 1966 calling for Black pride, self-determination and control of Black communities
a Black religious movement based in Chicago that Malcolm X joined in prison and left in 1964
a group founded in Oakland in 1966 that combined armed police patrols with community programs

look.title: Two Societies
look.text: Our nation is moving toward two societies, one black, one white—separate and unequal.
look.cite: Report of the National Advisory Commission on Civil Disorders (the Kerner Commission), U.S. government, 1968
look.prompt: This federal commission studied the riots of 1967 in Detroit, Newark and other cities. Three years after the Voting Rights Act, why might a government report have reached such a bleak conclusion?

choices: He supported gradual integration through the courts
He worked mainly in the rural South
He argued for nonviolence only

check.why: Until 1964 Malcolm X mocked integration and insisted on the right to strike back.

check.q: What changed Malcolm X's thinking in 1964?
choices: His pilgrimage to Mecca and break with the Nation of Islam
A meeting with President Johnson
The March on Washington

check.why: After Mecca, where he prayed alongside Muslims of all races, he began to revise his views on race and reach out to other leaders.

Organizing the Selma march
Publishing Jet magazine
check.why: The Panthers combined armed self-defense with community services like breakfast programs.

lessons.title: The Movements That Followed
lessons.mainIdea: The methods and laws of the Black freedom struggle were taken up by women, Latinos, Native Americans, people with disabilities and gay Americans.
reading: The Civil Rights Act's one-word addition, sex, gave the women's movement a legal lever. In 1966 Betty Friedan and others founded the National Organization for Women to make the government enforce it. Title IX in 1972 barred sex discrimination in schools that took federal money and transformed girls' sports. Congress passed the Equal Rights Amendment that year, but it fell short of ratification by enough states before its deadline; Illinois did not ratify it until 2018. Women's share of law and medical students, tiny in 1960, was near half by the century's end.

In California, farmworkers led by Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta struck the grape growers of Delano in 1965 and asked the nation to boycott grapes. The strike lasted five years and won the first union contracts for field workers. In Chicago, Puerto Rican young people in Lincoln Park formed the Young Lords in 1968 to fight displacement of their neighborhood. Native American activists founded the American Indian Movement in 1968, occupied Alcatraz Island in 1969, and in 1975 won a federal law giving tribes more control over their own programs.

People with disabilities used the sit-in directly. In 1977 protesters occupied a federal building in San Francisco for nearly a month until the government issued rules under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, which banned discrimination by programs that received federal money. Judy Heumann, who had been denied a teaching license because she used a wheelchair, was a leader. In 1975 Congress required public schools to educate every child with a disability, the law now called IDEA, which is why students have individualized education plans today. In 1990 the Americans with Disabilities Act extended the ban to private businesses, public transit and employment.

In June 1969 patrons of the Stonewall Inn, a gay bar in New York, fought back against a police raid, and the anniversary became the first pride marches the next year, including one in Chicago. Illinois had been the first state to repeal its law against private homosexual conduct, in 1961. Over the following decades the movement won the removal of homosexuality from the list of mental illnesses, protections against discrimination in many states, and in 2015 the Supreme Court's ruling in Obergefell v. Hodges that same-sex couples have the right to marry. Each of these movements borrowed the sit-in, the march, the lawsuit and the boycott, and each argued that the Fourteenth Amendment's promise belonged to it too.

words.d: the 1972 law banning sex discrimination in schools that receive federal money
a proposed constitutional amendment guaranteeing equal rights regardless of sex, passed by Congress in 1972 but never fully ratified
the 1973 rule that programs receiving federal money may not discriminate against people with disabilities
the 1990 law banning disability discrimination in jobs, businesses and public services
the New York bar where a 1969 police raid sparked the modern gay rights movement

look.title: The Ramp
look.text: Look at the front door of your school. Is there a ramp beside the steps, an elevator inside, a button that opens the door? None of those existed in most public buildings in 1970. Someone had to argue, in a sit-in or a courtroom, that a student who uses a wheelchair has the same right to enter as anyone else, and someone had to pay for the concrete.
look.prompt: Choose one feature of your school that exists because of a law from this lesson. Which strategy from the Black freedom movement helped win it?

check.q: How did the Civil Rights Act of 1964 help the women's movement?
choices: It gave women the vote
It created Title IX
Its ban on job discrimination included sex, which women's groups then pushed the government to enforce
It required equal pay in all states
check.why: The word sex in the employment section became the legal lever that groups like NOW used.

check.q: What did the 1977 sit-in in San Francisco achieve?
choices: Passage of the Americans with Disabilities Act
Rules enforcing Section 504's ban on disability discrimination in federally funded programs
The end of the grape boycott
The founding of the American Indian Movement
check.why: After nearly a month, the government issued the Section 504 regulations. The ADA came in 1990.

check.q: What did all of these later movements have in common with the Black freedom struggle?
choices: They all began in Chicago
They were led by the same organizations
They all won constitutional amendments
They used sit-ins, marches, boycotts and lawsuits and claimed the Fourteenth Amendment's promise
check.why: Each borrowed the movement's tactics and its legal argument about equal protection.

lessons.title: Strategies and Costs
lessons.mainIdea: The movement won by combining courts, direct action, media and the vote, and it paid in lives, jobs, and years that its participants never got back.
reading: Step back and the movement's toolkit becomes visible. Lawyers built the legal foundation, from Brown to Browder to the cases that enforced the 1964 and 1965 acts. Direct action created crises that could not be ignored: the empty buses, the occupied counters, the burned bus, the children in Birmingham. Organizers did the slow work in between, registering voters door to door and training people to endure. And television carried the images to a national audience whose opinion moved Congress. No single tool worked alone. The debates inside the movement, between lawyers and marchers, between King and SNCC, between nonviolence and Black Power, were arguments about which tool to use next.

The costs were not spread evenly. Medgar Evers, Jimmie Lee Jackson, James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, Michael Schwerner, James Reeb, Viola Liuzzo, the four girls in Birmingham, Malcolm X, Fred Hampton and Martin Luther King Jr. were all killed. Hundreds of others were beaten or bombed. Thousands lost jobs, homes and farms for registering to vote or hosting a volunteer. Many young organizers left the South in the late 1960s with injuries, nightmares and broken health. The FBI, under J. Edgar Hoover, wiretapped King, tried to discredit him, and ran a program to disrupt Black organizations.

The results were real and incomplete. Legal segregation is gone; a Black student from Chicago can ride any bus and eat at any counter in Mississippi. Black voters and officeholders exist in numbers unthinkable in 1954. Yet the problems King found in Chicago, housing, schools tied to housing, and the wealth gap that both produce, remain. Historians measure the movement by both columns: what changed in the law, and what the law could not reach.

The best way to weigh it is with evidence. Compare the registration tables of 1964 and 1968. Read the Kerner Commission's warning of two societies in the same year as the Fair Housing Act. Look at a map of Chicago neighborhoods by race today next to a redlining map from the 1930s. Listen to an oral history from a Freedom Summer volunteer, now in their eighties. The movement is not a finished story with a moral. It is a set of choices people made under pressure, and the same choices are still available.

words.d: a set of strategies; the movement's included lawsuits, direct action, organizing and media
a secret FBI program from 1956 to 1971 that spied on and disrupted civil rights and other political groups
the difference in what families own; a lasting effect of housing discrimination

look.title: The Ledger
look.text: Draw two columns on a page. On the left list what the movement changed between 1954 and 1968: laws, court rulings, who could vote, who could sit where. On the right list what it cost: names, jobs, homes, years. Then add a third column for what it did not reach.
look.prompt: Using evidence from this chapter, which column is longest? Does the length of a column tell you whether the movement was worth it, or do you need a different measure?
